Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

The latter shrinks down that same technology into a ring, albeit one that isn't going to be available in the US. If you're unfamiliar, Natural Cycles made its name with its FDA-cleared health app offering "digital birth control."

The older unit was designed to be worn only while sleeping, monitoring the wearer's heart rate, movement and temperature. Its successor, however, is a general-purpose activity tracker which can be worn day and night, adding additional insights into its user's health.

There have also been plenty of improvements to the hardware, with the Band 2 far smaller and lighter than its predecessor. Despite the smaller form factor and all-day wear, the battery life has increased from 14 days to 21. It's also a lot hardier, being able to withstand being immersed in water to depths of up to 50 meters.

The new NC Band 2 is available to pre-order today, priced at $149 alongside a year's app plan, or $99 for existing users. It is HSA/FSA eligible and the company expects it to begin shipping at some point in December.

Of more interest, but not available in America, is the NC Ring, which begins shipping today in Canada, Europe and Australia. Measuring 2.43mm thick and 5.8mm wide, it's designed to keep an eye on its user's temperature and movement. It doesn't ship with an optical heart rate sensor both to reduce any night-time distractions and to keep the battery life running for up to 14 days on a charge. Like its wrist-worn siblings, it'll connect via Bluetooth to the Natural Cycles app to offer up more data for fertility and cycle tracking.

If you're wondering why Natural Cycles isn't selling the ring in the US, your guess is as good as ours. It certainly wouldn't do to speculate as to why it would choose to ignore such a lucrative and vast market. #259. Router VPN vs. VPN app: How are these setups different?

Should you install a VPN on your router or your devices?

If you're a frequent VPN user, you may have an app installed on each one of your devices. But many routers these days have built-in support for VPN connections too. In theory, this means you can simply connect your router to the VPN and route internet traffic from every connected device on your network through the encrypted tunnel.

But even though a router-level VPN connection sounds like a good idea, it has its own set of drawbacks. While it can save you from managing individual connections, routing your household's internet traffic through a VPN on your router can lead to slower speeds.

Having said that, not every device supports VPN connections, so tunneling your router is often your only option. That raises an important question: When does it make sense to use a VPN on your router, and when are individual apps the better option?

There are good reasons to connect your router directly to a VPN instead of configuring each individual device. The first one is that you don't have to install apps on different devices, sign in to your account and remember to enable the tunnel every single time. Many of the best VPN services also restrict how many devices can connect at once. Your router takes up just one slot while routing traffic from all devices on your network through the VPN.

Most VPN providers have dedicated apps for major operating systems including Windows, macOS, Android, iOS and even Linux. However, many devices that would benefit from a VPN connection, including game consoles like the Nintendo Switch and the PlayStation 5, don't offer support for it. Take smart TVs, for instance. Even though you might want to use a VPN for streaming apps like Netflix, many mainstream TV operating systems such as Samsung's Tizen and LG's webOS don't offer any VPN settings whatsoever. One of the ways to get around this would be to use a VPN-capable streaming device like an Nvidia Shield.

Finally, some routers have excellent VPN policy controls that allow you to selectively route certain website domains or devices through the encrypted tunnel. For example, you could choose to only route your smart TV's traffic or Netflix-related data through a VPN. Very few routers support this functionality, though.

Many websites also block connections originating from VPN servers, which is why most people don't leave a VPN running at all times. For example, you may notice Google search often requires completing a CAPTCHA when you access it through a VPN. Other websites may fail to load entirely, leaving you with an HTTP 403 or 401 error. With a device-level connection, you can quickly disable the VPN to load a stubborn website.

Not every router is powerful enough to handle VPN encryption at high speeds. In practical terms, this means you may see a severe reduction in bandwidth with a VPN enabled on your router. Your smartphone or computer is significantly more powerful, so a device-level VPN connection can make full use of your internet connection instead of being bottlenecked to slower speeds.

While using a VPN on individual devices offers these advantages, note that each device takes up one connection slot, so you may want to keep the number of simultaneous connections down to a minimum. Leaving a VPN running all the time on your phone or laptop can also lead to battery drain, but with an app, you can switch it off whenever you don't need it.

#258. They Defeated a Strongman. But Can They Run a Country?

Serbia’s student movement was deliberately leaderless and made group decisions to unseat Aleksandar Vucic. Now no one seems quite sure what happens next.

They had no leader, no political party and no conventional campaign. They made decisions by raising their hands after hours of debate in university classrooms, a slow and cumbersome process billed as a unique experiment in direct democracy.

That free-form approach to politics of Serbia’s students proved so effective that, in a general election on Oct. 25, they achieved what established opposition parties had failed to accomplish for more than a decade: routing the well-oiled political machine of Serbia’s strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic.

Mr. Vucic, nearing the end of his second term as president and barred from running again, had resigned as president a month before the October vote for a new Parliament, gambling that his governing party would win and that he could keep his grip on power by becoming prime minister. He had held that post twice before.

His plan was upended by the election victory of a slate of parliamentary candidates selected by students in freewheeling campus meetings. Their selections and electoral successes marked the culmination of a striking exercise in collective decision making. That approach, some believe, could hold lessons for democratic movements beyond Serbia.

But the principles that carried the students to victory may not, on their own, be enough to build a functioning, coherent and durable government.

The diverse list of candidates chosen by the students, nearly all political novices with a wide range of sometimes contradictory views, reflected a belief that everyone should have a say in a leaderless movement united by the single objective of getting rid of Mr. Vucic and the system he created.

#256. Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse

Robotics startup misses payroll a year after CEO used funds for luxury home.

A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza.

Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC. The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago.

This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.

The company has demonstrated a humanoid robot named the Phantom MK-1 and is touting an upcoming robot called the Phantom MK-2. Foundation has touted its humanoid robots for roles in warehouses and other workplaces—but has courted media coverage by claiming it is developing humanoid robots for battlefield use.

Now CNBC’s reporting based on “people with direct knowledge of the matter” indicates that insiders worry the startup could soon collapse without additional funding.

Eric Trump holds an equity stake in Foundation and was announced as its chief strategy advisor in March 2026, according to the Financial Times. Investment funds linked to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are involved with multiple military technology companies that have received Pentagon loans and contracts worth more than $3.2 billion as of July 2026, according to The Washington Post.

After Trump claimed that Foundation had “just secured a $24 million contract with the Pentagon” during the Fox Business interview in April, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) responded by questioning whether the Pentagon is “just a cash machine for Trump’s kids now” in a social media post. “This looks like corruption in plain sight,” Warren wrote.

But publicly available evidence does not back up Trump’s claim about Foundation directly receiving US government funding. Federal spending records show that Foundation holds no publicly listed contracts, according to The San Francisco Standard.

Instead, the company Boardwalk Robotics received four contracts worth $3.22 million prior to being acquired by Foundation in late 2024.

Meanwhile, the Institute for Human & Machine Cognition—a Florida-based nonprofit research institute and research partner to Boardwalk Robotics—secured a $24.8 million Navy contract in 2025, The San Francisco Standard reported.

This was not the first time that Foundation’s leadership and investors have made unsupported statements. In 2024, General Motors pushed back on Foundation’s claims that it was about to get an investment from the Detroit automaker, according to CNBC.

On November 11, 2026, Mike LeBlanc, co-founder and president of Foundation Future Industries, told the Financial Times that the company was in talks with the Israeli military to provide humanoid robots for patrol and combat duties in Hamas tunnels beneath Gaza. He also described taking the company’s Phantom MK1 humanoid robot along to tour some of the tunnels.

However, the Israeli defense ministry declined to comment when the Financial Times reached out.

LeBlanc also previously claimed that two of the company’s Phantom MK-1 units went to Ukraine for testing in frontline reconnaissance and logistics roles in February 2026.

But Craig Smith, an independent journalist and host of the podcast Eye on AI, described tagging along during the delivery of the Phantom robots to Ukraine. He said that the robots never made it to Ukraine because they were stopped at the border with Poland.

When questioned by Smith, LeBlanc only said that Foundation had conducted a pilot demonstration at an undisclosed location, without clarifying whether the robots ever reached Ukraine. LeBlanc also walked back a claim that Foundation had demonstrated its humanoid robots to the Ukrainian government organization Brave1.

Promotional videos showing Foundation’s humanoids have not provided evidence that the robots are ready for battlefield deployments. For example, a “mortar demo” video on the company website dated to May 2026 shows a person handing a mortar shell to one of the humanoid robots, which slowly lowers the shell over the muzzle of a mortar weapon before finally dropping it in.

Whatever happens to Foundation, humanoid robots remain largely unproven technology and have yet to fulfill company promises that they can become general-purpose robots handling many different tasks. Companies have just begun testing and deploying such robots in greater numbers within relatively controlled environments such as factories and warehouses.

Similarly, humanoid robots have not yet had any impact on the battlefield. Instead, pioneers in robotics warfare, like the Ukrainian military, have focused on developing and deploying unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs)—robotic vehicles that roll along on wheels or tank-style caterpillar tracks.

While defending against the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Ukrainian military has increasingly deployed more ground robots along with swarms of flying drones to make up for a shortfall in human soldiers compared to Russia. Such ground robots have typically been tasked with performing risky supply runs or evacuating wounded soldiers from frontline positions, but have also entered combat while wielding projectile weapons or even explosives when equipped as roving bombs.

Most recently, Ukraine has deployed armed ground robots directly into combat through both amphibious landings and through airdrops. In 2026, part of Ukraine’s counteroffensive success in rolling back Russian territorial gains has included dropping military robots from drones in airborne assaults behind Russian frontline positions.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#254. 5 important Bose headphone settings that need to be manually turned on

Pairing your Bose headphones is just the beginning. A few small tweaks in the companion app's settings can make your headphones feel more like yours.

Bose has made some of the most popular headphones around for years, but even if you've been using them for a while, you may not be getting everything you can out of yours. The company's headphones are perfectly capable of producing great sound right out of the box, but some of their best features actually have to be activated manually. Whether there's something you always wished your headphones could do or you just want to see if they can perform even better, it's worth exploring settings like an equalizer, multi-connection support, noise canceling, shortcuts to your favorite features, or sidetone settings.

Keep in mind that not every pair of Bose headphones will have access to all of these settings. Newer QuietComfort models are upgraded in all the right places, offering a few unique features, while first-generation QuietComfort Ultra and QuietComfort headphones lack some of those features. You'll also need to download the Bose app to tweak anything beyond their basic settings, as the controls on the headphones themselves are pretty minimal.

One useful feature on compatible Bose headphones is the equalizer (EQ). Like with any piece of audio equipment, the equalizer lets you modify different sound frequencies to your taste, like adjusting the audio quality in Apple Music, letting you pump up the bass or improving the high end so it's brighter. Reviews often call out Bose for boosting bass too much out of the box, so it may be a good idea to try turning it down a touch before making other adjustments.

Bose's equalizer only lets you change volume across three bands — bass, mid and treble — but that's plenty for most users without making it too complex. There are also preset options to choose from if you want to take Bose's recommendations or pick one to start with and customize your profile from there. You'll find the equalizer on the home screen of the Bose app, under EQ.

One of the more annoying aspects of using Bluetooth headphones is having to disconnect and reconnect them whenever you want to switch from one device to another. Bluetooth multipoint lets Bluetooth devices connect to multiple sources at once, so you can switch between them without disconnecting and reconnecting. Compatible Bose headphones have this feature, but you have to enable it in the app.

You'll find Bluetooth multipoint in the Settings section of the app, under Bluetooth Connections. Just toggle it on, and you'll be able to connect your headphones to two different audio sources. To switch devices, pause the audio on one and press play on the other, or swap between them in the app if the switch doesn't happen. Like basically everything to do with Bluetooth, multipoint connection doesn't always work perfectly, but it's extremely convenient when it does.

Bose features some serious pros of using noise-canceling headphones. You can choose from a few modes to adjust how noise-canceling works, with newer models adding more modes. QuietComfort Ultra headphones turn on in Quiet mode by default, but if you find an option you like better, you can set the app to remember the last mode used through the app's Settings menu.

Under the Modes menu in the app, you'll find at least two different noise-canceling presets, depending on which headphones you have. Quiet (full noise cancellation) and Aware (full transparency) are available on the QuietComfort Ultra headphones. In newer headphones, Immersion mode aims to replicate the experience of music being played from a stage in front of you, and Cinema mode enhances dialogue clarity while you're watching movies and TV. You can also define multiple custom modes by choosing which specific noise-canceling features to activate.

Many Bose headphones let you customize their controls, though the specifics will obviously depend on which model you own. QuietComfort Ultra headphones have a touch-sensitive strip, and older headphone models offer the Action Button, both of which can activate your chosen shortcut.

To set the behavior of the custom control, check the Shortcut option in the app. Depending on your model, this will let you choose from a few options, including hearing the battery level as it changes, changing the Immersive Audio mode and switching between previously connected Bluetooth devices. For headphones, you can only set one, but some earbuds let you assign a different shortcut to each ear. If you don't use shortcuts and don't want to risk accidentally activating them, you can also turn them off completely in the app.

A somewhat more niche feature comes in the form of Self Voice. If you've ever taken a call while wearing headphones, especially noise-canceling ones, you might be familiar with how strange it can be to hear your own voice muffled as you speak. By default, Bose headphones feed a certain amount of your own voice back to you to make speaking feel more natural, otherwise known as sidetone.

The Self Voice feature in the app lets you adjust just how much comes through, but you won't find it on the home screen. Instead, tap the Settings gear icon and look for Self Voice there, where you can set it to High, Medium or Low, or turn it off completely. As long as it's not turned off, Self Voice activates automatically during calls, so you don't need to manually toggle it on.

#253. Xiaomi's 18 Pro series can generate vibe-coded apps for its tiny rear display

The cameras don’t seem to reach the dizzying heights of last year’s 17 Ultra.

Xiaomi's premium smartphone series has been in great form in recent years. Alongside last year's 17 Ultra (and its Leica-collab camera), it launched its own passport-shaped foldable, the technically impressive 18 Fold, just before Apple debuted the iPhone Duo.

Its new phones, the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, combine a more advanced rear display with some of the company's latest innovations found on the 17 Ultra and its foldables. Naturally, because it's 2026, that includes a serving of AI assistance and generative AI, but Xiaomi brought some genuinely smart ideas to the latter. The Pro series is launching in more regions this year, including the UK and other parts of Western Europe, but still won't come to the US. The 18 Pro Max is priced at £1400 (roughly $1,850) and the 18 Pro at £1,199 (around $1,580), continuing this year's upward trajectory of smartphone prices. Both are priced higher than Xiaomi's flagship (and my favorite camera phone), the 17 Ultra.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch main display and a slightly larger 2.9-inch rear display. The 18 Pro, meanwhile, has a 6.40-inch screen with a 2.7-inch rear display. The Pro Max model also features Snapdragon's new 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip, with up to 16 gigs of RAM, while the 18 Pro has a (still powerful) Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 with 12GB of RAM.

There are also battery capacity differences between the two phones. The Xiaomi 18 Pro has a 6,000mAh cell with 90W max charging, but if you're demanding more battery life, the Pro Max has a larger 7,050mAh battery and 100W fast charging.

The hardware feels decidedly premium, complemented by a couple of vivid color options, including a gorgeous Velvet Red finish last seen on Xiaomi's latest foldable. Both phones will also come in Black, White and Cosmic Blue colors. Even if you choose the vivid red or blue models, it's the small back display that catches the eye first.

The Back Display uses the same display tech as the Xiaomi 18 Pro series' screen, peaking at 4,000-nit brightness and up to 120Hz refresh rates, though chances of seeing those upper limits are probably few and far between. Both the back display and camera array are protected with a single Corning Gorilla Glass Victus cover, making a surprisingly busy back look a little more cohesive.

The Back Display's functions fall into two main categories. First, like the flip foldables we've seen in recent years, it works as a display for the phone's primary cameras. The back display's viewfinder automatically switches to ultra-wide if it spots three or more people in the shot, but otherwise it's a stripped-down version of the camera app. While it makes sense, given the smaller screen space for buttons and modes, it relegates many shooting modes and features to the main camera app on the phone's main screen.

Alongside the notifications and information feeds we've seen on phones like Samsung's Z Flip series and Motorola's Razr phones, including calls, maps and weather, Xiaomi adds a pin-to-back function that lets you attach text and images for quick reference. The company suggests pinning boarding passes and QR codes, but you could also add a cute pic of family or pets. It's also the first rear display to support apps like Spotify, YouTube Music and Google Maps – hopefully more apps will join those. Xiaomi said Gemini Live can run on the rear display, but I haven't been able to get it to work on my 18 Pro yet.

The new feature on this year's Back Display lets you program your own mini apps, similar to how you can program the iPhone's recent AI-infused Shortcuts. Using GenAI, you can describe a lightweight app or function, and the Xiaomi 18 Pro will attempt to make it a reality. It's a clever way to sidestep the difficulty of getting app developers on board with niche screen sizes and proportions. Xiaomi promises over 50 preset apps at launch, although the selection was much more limited on the Xiaomi 17 Pro I've been using.

It's not about making dense, full-size apps, but rather simple, single-purpose (interactive) widgets. There's something to this idea, but I couldn't quite get apps to behave or look the way I wanted. One idea: a faux wallpaper that would generate screen cracks and glitches when touched. Regardless of how many times I asked the phone not to include an on-screen crack counter, ruining the appeal of my lame 'prank', subsequent vibe-coded builds still featured a counter.

I also tried to create a guess-the-flag quiz, but it seemed to lean heavily on the 25 or so countries that most of us could answer, easily. When I asked it to increase the flag range by 100 more, the phone struggled to generate a new mini app, even though I assumed it was an easy expansion of the initial premise. There are some smart implementations, including a button to 'polish' the idea you wrote to make it more palatable to generative AI.

It's a little sluggish to both refine and generate these mini-apps, especially if you've dipped your toe into genAI coding elsewhere, which is usually pretty swift. The feature requires an internet connection to work and it's not entirely clear whether they're generated on-device, which might explain slower processing.

Wallpaper options for the tiny rear display also include AI Group photo wallpapers, which I'm less sold on, which combine two different subjects into a group photo. You can even create composite portraits of celebrities and fictional characters – maybe this just isn't for me. I'll go back to my flag guessing.

Cameras are once again a priority for Xiaomi. Both phones have dual 200-megapixel camera systems, with Leica Summilux lenses. The 18 Pro Max has a 200MP Light Fusion 960L primary sensor with LOFIC technology, which delivers more dynamic range to protect highlights and boost low-light performance. The 18 Pro, however, uses the same 200MP Light Fusion 960 sensor, minus the LOFIC part. Both have an f/1.67 lens and optical image stabilization.

The periscope telephoto is also 200MP, with an f/2.4 lens, OIS and 3.2x optical zoom, extending to 12.8x in-sensor cropped zoom. There's a 50MP ultrawide too, separately nestled below the other two cameras. This makes for a more sensible-looking camera array alongside the back display, the very opposite of Motorola's tryptophobia-inducing Signature 17.

I've been testing the 18 Pro's cameras for only a few days (and the 18 Pro Max is arriving today, so I'll have updated impressions soon). Performance doesn't reach the high expectations set by last year's 17 Ultra, with its massive 1-inch sensor. While daylight shots and macro landscapes remain crisp, the standard Pro often struggled to capture moving subjects and low-light scenes. The Pro Max-exclusive LOFIC sensor could bridge that gap, however, so I'll update this story if it does.

Leica's Essential Moments is an enjoyable shooting mode in the camera app, evolving from a single-camera mode to multiple styles and even lens options. It's a little different from the Leica camera simulations on Xiaomi's flagships last year. Powered by Xiaomi's own large model photography engine, the shooting mode applies one of three Leica-inspired color grades. You can also shoot through two "classic lens" simulations based on 35mm and 75mm lenses. Xiaomi has distilled it down to three styles, and I've always liked the old-school CCD tones of Leica cameras. As I've said in other reviews and hands-ons, Xiaomi and Leica seem to have nailed this, including a monochrome mode (which, again, is great), while keeping it curated to just three distinct looks.

There are all the other shooting modes you'd expect, too, with Xiaomi's pro shooting mode another standout. Focus peaking and exposure highlights are baked in, and you can refine your own filter parameters, including adding noise grain and hue.

For now, Xiaomi's 17 Ultra remains its true photography flagship, but the 18 Pro series still delivers impressive results and, crucially, a fun shooting experience. In the UK, both phones are available to order from Xiaomi and Amazon.

#252. Searching for the Last Stoats of Waiheke Island

Can the tourist destination become the first urban island to rid itself of the stoat — an introduced predator that has ravaged New Zealand’s endemic wildlife?

Can the tourist destination become the first urban island to rid itself of the stoat — an introduced predator that has ravaged New Zealand’s endemic wildlife?

Frank Lepera, stoat operations manager at Te Korowai o Waiheke, installing a trap where a stoat was recently reported, on Waiheke Island, New Zealand.Credit...

Reporting from Waiheke Island, New Zealand. She did not see a live stoat on the island.

To catch a stoat, you need to think like one. For Tilde Sorensen, that means imagining having tiny legs and picturing which route the weasel-like creature might take as it haunts the wilderness of New Zealand, preying on unique birdlife.

“We’ve caught all of the ones that will happily go into a trap. So now we’ve got to figure out how to get the really shy ones,” Ms. Sorensen said of the stoat population on Waiheke Island, a 40-minute boat ride from New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland.

“We’re trying to work ourselves out of a job.”

Ms. Sorensen is a stoat-detect-and-respond coordinator for a project called Te Korowai o Waiheke, a Māori name that means The Cloak of Waiheke. It has captured more than 280 stoats since 2020 and, while it is not known how many remain, testing suggests the population has dwindled.

The campaign to eradicate stoats, and many other introduced species, has widespread support in New Zealand, where introduced predators, including rats and possums, kill about 25 million native birds each year.

Waiheke Island, which covers about 36 square miles, is home to 4,300 people, a number that swells to about 45,000 in the summer.

#250. The hidden features every Google Maps user should know about

Most of us use Google Maps the same way day in and day out — we type in an address, follow the instructions and arrive at our destination. But the app also offers a lot of useful tools that aren't as easily accessible as telling it where to go. If you want to set a reminder for when to leave or ensure your music is uninterrupted while still getting the step-by-step instructions, there are settings you can change to make that happen. You can also turn Google Maps into a much more useful tool if you tell it what type of car you have, or specify your route settings all so you can get customized recommendations.

None of these features require a new app or a subscription, either. They are built directly into Google Maps, and you can get to them with a little bit of digging around, especially when you know where to look.

There's a feature within Google Maps that lets you specify what car you're driving. The make and model don't matter as much as what type of engine it has, letting you choose between gas, diesel, hybrid and electric. With this info, the app can tailor routing decisions to your car's needs.

For EV and plug-in hybrid owners, this feature is worth considering because you can tell Google Maps exactly what type of plug or adapter your car requires. This allows Maps to automatically surface compatible charging stations. You can find this setting in Settings > Your vehicles. Once set, you can search for charging stations along your route, and the app will signal those that will work with your specific car.

Route preferences deserve the same attention. The app's settings make it possible to toggle options to avoid tolls, ferries or even highways. This is useful if you'd rather take the scenic (or cheaper) route or if you wish to avoid the freeway at its higher speeds. To turn the feature on, go to Settings > Navigation, and you'll find all toggles under Route options. One thing that will save you time in the long run is setting or changing your home address on Google Maps so you can jump straight to your custom directions with a single tap. If you have your Gemini assistant enabled, you can even say "navigate home" and it will set the route for you.

Running late is rarely about the drive itself, but more about leaving at the wrong time. Unless an accident has delayed your journey, you probably left home late in accordance with your predicted arrival time — Google Maps is that good at estimating when you'll arrive based on your chosen route.

Well, you can use Google Maps on iPhone and its "Set a reminder to leave" feature to receive an alert telling you when to head out so you're not late for appointments. You can set an arrive-by time (or a leave-by time) for your destination under Directions > transportation mode and then tap the three-dot menu and select Set a reminder to leave > Depart or Arrive > set the time > Done. Maps will now notify you when to leave. On Android, things are a little different; to get the same results requires Google Calendar to set the reminder by creating an event with the appointment's date and time while adding the destination to the location field.

This feature shines best in busy cities where traffic on the same stretch of road can vary dramatically between a Monday afternoon and a Friday evening. For anyone juggling back-to-back meetings, school pickups and a million extracurricular activities, these reminders remove the need to check the app constantly. It's a quiet but dependable feature, and it's equally useful if you're planning on using public transport.

If you've ever had Spotify, a book or a podcast cut out midway to announce an upcoming exit, you know how annoying that can be. Thankfully, there's an easy fix if you'd like to silence Google Maps: you simply have to turn off the "Play voice over Bluetooth" setting, a fine way to improve your Android Auto experience. This will stop Google Maps from interrupting your music over your car's speakers, while still giving you visual turn-by-turn guidance on screen. The voice telling you to turn left or right will come from your phone rather than your car's speakers. It's a small adjustment that will make a big difference, especially if you drive in the city a lot and need to change direction often. To do this, go to your profile, scroll down to Settings and go to Navigation. The feature's toggle will be available up top, under Sound & Voice.

One cool perk that's worth knowing about when you're using Android Auto is that when you're parked at your destination or somewhere for a rest, you can take a breather and play games directly on an Android Auto screen. That could make the wait during your kid's next practice session a little more entertaining.

#248. Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on.”

Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.

She is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.

Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.

“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”

Rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.

For those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.

The 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.

To protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too quickly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.)

The only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.

After the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip, then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.

“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” said Rosen.

There has been a longstanding debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.

“It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream-white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” said Rosen.

By the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.

“And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen said.

It was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”

“If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she said.

“There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”

Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.

“She had to come up with a lot of new processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part, and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he said.

Some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.

“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and, I mean, I touched every inch of it,” Rosen said. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”

Even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.

Now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut, Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has launched her career into a new frontier.

“In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” said Rosen.

“So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she said.

The California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.

#247. Canada’s Leader, Once a Curiosity at Asia Summits, Is Now a Star

Prime Minister Mark Carney is courting Europe, but the bigger payoff might be in China, where he will share summit stages with Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and President Trump.

Reporting from Phnom Penh, Cambodia; Manila; and Dublin

The importance of Europe to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify Canada’s economy and politics away from its reliance on the United States was underscored last week by his travel schedule.

Mr. Carney added a stop in Dublin, joining a meeting of European leaders before the start of a previously planned trip to Asia.

Last month Mr. Carney announced that Canada is officially seeking to become the first “associate member” of the European Union. But experts say that Asia offers the greater economic opportunity.

“Prime Minister Carney certainly seems to have a strong focus on Europe, which gives an impression that he is not looking toward Asia,” said Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of public policy. “Nevertheless, if Canada is to avoid dependence on the U.S. market and form a coalition of middle powers, cooperation with Asia is essential.”

Last year, Mr. Carney was something of a curiosity at the meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. But his speech in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and President Trump’s addition of energy security threats to his trade war with the world have made Mr. Carney and his energy-rich country a marquee attraction at both.

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS says.

He was sentenced to life in a secure hospital in December 2023 because of his autism, but in January, Kurtaj was deemed fit for trial and moved to prison, the BBC reports.

Kurtaj is set to be sentenced on November 23rd. GTA VI will be released on November 19th.

#245. Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#243. Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it

AI agent takes unapproved actions even when laptop lid is closed and told not to.

Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.

The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.

Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”

The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.

“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Ido Hoorvitch, a NewCore security researcher, wrote in an email. “A vulnerability gets fixed. This is the product working as designed: an agent that holds your credentials, acts under your identity while you sleep, ignores the one refusal you can give it, and then tells you it did nothing.”

Hoorvitch said that Grok Bot provides minimal notification of the automatic “turns,” or the cycles that occur when an agent receives instructions or context, decides what to do, and calls whatever tools it chooses. The notice comes during onboarding when the bot says it keeps working while the user is away from the computer and connects to apps and uses them the way the user does.

“It reads like a welcome message and scrolls off the screen in under a minute,” Hoorvitch said. “Nobody is asked to consent to it. Nothing says the platform will start turns with no message from you, or that those turns will use your connectors.”

The researcher said that Grok Bot documentation notes that a primary bot checks in on its own, and a changelog mentions brief background wakes, but there is no mention that the check-ins “reach into your connected apps.” Further, once a check-in runs, there is no mention of it in the chat interface or in the chat history, and as already noted, prompts to stop check-ins don’t work. Hoorvitch said the bot “always asks before making changes,” but that applies only to events in which data or changes are written to an app.

NewCore contacted Grok Bot support on November 4. At the time, users had no way to turn off the automatic check-ins. Then, eight days later, Hoorvitch said, the Cursor dashboard, the administrative console behind Grok Bot, received an update. Under bot capabilities, a new toggle called proactive messages appeared. By default, it’s set to on. When a team admin sets it to off, bots no longer run check-ins on their own.

SpaceXSI representatives didn’t answer questions sent by email.

#242. American Global Health Aid Isn’t Dead. It’s Changing.

The Trump administration promised to make aid programs more “America First.” Some countries are balking.

Americans might have assumed that their country was out of the business of promoting global health. On his first day in office, President Trump announced the United States’ withdrawal from the World Health Organization and abruptly “paused” foreign aid. Over the following weeks, Elon Musk took a chain saw to the U.S. Agency for International Development.

In the wake of these actions, reporters documented shortages of tuberculosis, malaria and H.I.V. drugs, widespread clinic closures and the abandonment of patients enrolled in medical trials. Many programs never resumed, and researchers predicted that hundreds of thousands of avoidable deaths would occur in the first year alone. Assessing whether this came true is complicated by the fact that programs tracking health outcomes were among those the U.S. ended.

Congress had originally allocated about $10 billion to the government’s main global health programs, or roughly $30 per U.S. resident, to run one of the world’s most effective foreign aid efforts. But even after the wave of staff terminations and grant cancellations, Congress still wanted that money to be spent. To direct the funds, last September, the U.S. State Department released a new plan: the America First Global Health Strategy.

This plan endorsed some goals that experts have long championed regardless of political fealty, such as having recipient countries take more responsibility for running and funding the programs.

But it also had a distinctly Trumpian element that seemed shocking to observers of the foreign aid world: The money had significant — and unusual — strings attached. Countries that receive aid were invited to negotiate “America First” agreements with the United States “that promote our national interests while saving millions of lives,” according to a letter from Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

#241. The Verge Best of 2026

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Hundreds of gadgets pass across our desks each year. Some leave their mark and get a full review or make it to the top of a buying guide. It’s harder than it sounds to narrow down our favorites. Instead of simply picking products that scored highly, or only those that made it into our buying guides, we asked our reviews team and staff at large to nominate their products of the year. Then our editors whittled the list down to the top 25, balancing categories like smart home, phones, laptops, and just cool stuff.

The result is our Best of 2026 — a list of products our staff has purchased, reviewed, or just plain loves. It’s still mid-November, and we know new products are set to launch before the end of the year. So we may update this list if there’s anything we think deserves a spot before the ball drops on New Year’s Eve. Then we dive right into CES and start all over again in 2027.

Without further ado… here are The Verge Best of 2026 winners.

The Saros 20 is one of Roborock’s current flagship floor cleaners, but it distinguishes itself from the rest of the company’s robovacs with a pair of extending leglike appendages on the underside. It uses those legs to boost itself over obstacles, like uneven transitions between rooms. It’s highly maneuverable, thanks to its use of spinning mop pads instead of a heavy roller, and without a lidar tower protruding out the top. The Saros 20 is just 3.13 inches tall, small enough to squeeze under most furniture. It’s also equipped with excellent obstacle avoidance, and it uses a split brush design underneath with a gap, allowing hair and fibers to get quickly sucked instead of tangled up in bristles. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter

The Navimow X430 came out on top of our robot lawnmower showdown earlier this year, and The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy said it was “by far” the best one she tested. It was the only one that could mow her front and back yards in one trip, and the only one that didn’t get stuck. It even successfully rolled through potholes and over small tree branches. The Navimow X430’s 17-inch cutting width was also wider than the competition, helping it finish mowing faster. It navigates using a combination of technologies, but there’s also a handy remote control mode you can use to take over in sensitive spots in your yard, or to clean up stray grass fronds the bot missed. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer

The Fairphone 6 Plus is just a regular old Android phone, and that’s actually a triumph. Fairphone has been selling its repairable, ethically sourced phones for years now, and previous generations have been underpowered or come with serious compromises. The Fairphone 6 Plus doesn’t feel compromised in the same way, and it comes with swappable back panels with different accessories, like a wallet or grip. The $649 price feels entirely reasonable for what it offers, especially when you consider that you can take care of easy fixes, like swapping in a new battery yourself at minimal cost. In a year when we got a lot of bad RAMageddon-related news in the smartphone industry, the Fairphone 6 Plus felt like a relief. — Allison Johnson, senior reviewer

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max easily secured a spot on our Best of 2026 list. Apple didn’t change much in its winning formula this year but focused on what people care about most: camera and battery life. The biggest update is probably the main camera, which now has a variable aperture that lets photographers adjust background blur and take better low-light photos. The iPhone 18 Pro Max also has the longest battery life in an iPhone to date, while the iPhone 18 Pro lasts as long as last year’s 17 Pro Max. — Todd Haselton, deputy reviews editor

Before there was the iPhone Duo, there was the Z Fold 8. Not by much — just a few months — but Samsung beat Apple to market with a passport-shaped foldable. It’s a little thinner, lighter, and narrower than the Duo, and that makes a real difference in how comfortable it is to use for long stretches of time. It’s not rated for the same level of dust resistance as the Duo, and it doesn’t feel quite as “premium,” but apps make better use of the cover screen. The more I hold it, the more I think Apple needs to take a page out of Samsung’s book here. — Allison Johnson, senior reviewer

3D printing is finally something I can recommend to just about anyone with space for a 30-inch cube in their garage, because the Bambu Lab P2S Combo is the easiest printing experience I’ve touched. It prints beautifully out of the box but, more importantly, it keeps on printing with minimal care, maintenance, or fuss. I can leave rolls of colorful filament inside for months, then press a button on my phone to print, because the bundled AMS keeps them dry and automatically loads each one. Technically the P2S arrived in 2025, but I’d never buy a just-released 3D printer: I spent a year and over 1,700 hours of print time (and counting) to be sure of my recommendation. Wish Bambu treated the open-source community better, though. — Sean Hollister, senior editor

When The Verge decided to do a Best of 2026, my mind immediately jumped to the nerdiest thing I’ve tested all year — a dongle that lets you power aging gadgets with the same USB-C cables that charge your laptop and phone. Lose your SNES power brick? Want to make a desktop monitor portable? Want to make a Game Boy run forever? Werewolf VFLEX can make those happen, and so much more. It’s like having a universal AC adapter, one you don’t even need to plug into the wall, because USB-C batteries are amazing. — Sean Hollister, senior editor

It’s no surprise that, given its provenance, the Fitbit Air is an excellent fitness tracker, even if its tracking capabilities don’t go as in depth as other devices. For $100, the Air comes with a thinner and more comfortable strap than Whoop’s bands, with a design that lets the sensor module be easily removed and swapped into other straps. Battery life is excellent, requiring just a handful of charges each month while the Air tracks metrics like steps, heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen, and cardio load. All of that data is available through the Google Health app without a subscription, but for $100 you can upgrade to Google Health Premium, which adds access to video workouts, adaptive fitness plans, and an AI health coach that can share summaries of your day or night and answer questions about your health. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter

I usually regret my TikTok shop purchases. Not this one. I was tired of filling my journals with muddy, blue-tinged photos from HP Sprocket that faded over time. The Liene Pearl N200 Pro uses dye sublimation, so the colors are super vivid. The app is easy to use, and it comes with 50 sheets and five ink cartridges. You can usually find it for $100 to $120, and refills cost just $25 for 50 sheets. That’s pretty affordable — especially if you love scrapbooking. — Victoria Song, senior reviewer

The Oura Ring 5 is thinner and lighter than the Oura Ring 4. The metal finish is more durable than Oura’s previous models, so nicks and scratches should be less of an issue. The case also adds support for on-the-go wireless charging, but unfortunately it’s sold separately. This year’s Oura Ring also dropped the smallest and largest size options. The Oura Ring 5 is still the best smart ring on the market, especially if you’re upgrading from an older model or are new to smart rings. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer

2026 is the year nearly every TV manufacturer released an RGB LED TV, which uses individual red, green, and blue LEDs to provide the backlight instead of a field of blue or white LEDs. The Sony Bravia 9 II is the best of the bunch, with accurate, vibrant color; the incredible processing that Sony is known for; and a really cool lenticular screen on the stand that hides the cables behind it. The first generation of a new technology is always a bit tricky, but Sony showed that an RGB LED TV can be done right. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer

When Sony launched its WH-1000XM4C wireless headphones in October, there was a certain amount of smug satisfaction enjoyed by those of us who still prefer Sony’s six-year-old WH-1000XM4 headphones over its successors. Sony made significant design changes with the WH-1000XM5 and then walked a few of them back with the WH-1000XM6. Both have better active noise cancellation and battery life than Sony’s latest, but the new XM4C resurrects the XM4’s comfortable, compact folding design with a replaceable battery, so loyal fans of the original can enjoy the new version for years to come. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter

The Liberty 5 Pro set a new bar for call quality this year. The Verge’s John Higgins said they delivered the best in-call noise canceling he’s ever heard, even compared with pricier headphones like Apple’s AirPods Pro 3. They run on Anker’s new Thus chip and feature 9.2mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and IP55 water resistance. The case also has a built-in display to quickly change settings like ANC or check the Liberty 5 Pro’s battery life, with separate icons for each earbud and the case itself. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer

There’s plenty about the Studio Display XDR to find interesting: It’s the first Apple 5K monitor with a mini-LED panel and quantum dots that has a peak brightness of 2,000 nits, it has an adaptive refresh rate up to 120Hz, and it has a bunch of color-accurate reference modes for a wide range of professional uses. But what got me most excited was the inclusion of Apple’s CMF 2026 color-matching function for its two general picture-mode presets. It’s a new display standard developed as an alternative to CIE 1931, the standard for the past 80 years, which can cause colors to look different across multiple narrow-band display technologies like OLED and mini-LED with quantum dots. Apple CMF 2026 aims to fix that, and I’m here for it. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer

The MacBook Neo, despite running on an iPhone chip, works pretty darn well as a MacBook, and that’s mostly all I need to say. Yes, it now starts at $699 instead of $599 because of RAMageddon, so it’s not as good of a deal as it was when it launched. But it’s a very functional laptop, still has a great keyboard and (mechanical!) trackpad, and comes in fun colors. Apple hit it out of the park with the Neo. — Jay Peters, senior reporter

Framework’s Laptop 13 Pro is my ideal all-purpose Windows laptop (or Linux, if you’re inclined). It’s portable, powerful, dabbles in 1080p gaming, and it’s even user-upgradable and repairable. It’s the Framework formula many of us have come to love, like those precious modular ports, but with a major step up in quality-of-life features: a haptic trackpad, a nice touchscreen, and a much-improved build. Its biggest fault is its price. That’s the toll RAMageddon has taken on everything this year — it just hit a smaller manufacturer like Framework harder. Yes, Framework chose an extra-pricey component in LPCAMM2 memory, but that’s also part of why the 13 Pro is so cool and forward-looking. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer

I was so head over heels for the Ricoh GR IV Monochrome when I reviewed it that I recently bought one. A black-and-white-only fixed-lens camera is super niche, but for this photo nerd, it’s the perfect “artsy” pocket camera. I take it with me everywhere, even with my larger cameras during Verge events or wedding shoots. It’s a palate cleanser for everything from slice-of-life family snapshots to New York City street photography. I could achieve that with black-and-white film, but I inevitably fall off using my analog cameras. They say the best camera is the one you have with you, and the GR IV Monochrome is now always with me and always a delight. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer

The Nape Pro is the most unusual and best gadget I bought this year. It’s a bar-shaped device with six customizable buttons and a small trackball in the middle. I put it horizontally below my space bar, and once I tweaked the button layout, it became a daily driver. It feels like a cross between a trackpad and what I wish the TrackPoint on my ThinkPad was. The Nape Pro works over Bluetooth, USB-C, or 2.4GHz and supports up to 1000Hz polling. Battery life is fantastic, and it’s fully customizable. I still use a mouse at the big desk, but the Nape Pro is now as important to my portable setup as my laptop stand and keyboard. — Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor

Xteink redefined how small an e-reader can be, and while the company released several models in 2026 — including the X3, X4, and X4 Classic — the X4 Pro is the best of the bunch. It’s the company’s only model to include lighting and a touchscreen, which makes navigating Xteink’s software, or an excellent third-party alternative, much easier than using buttons alone. At $99, the X4 Pro is Xteink’s most expensive e-reader, and it doesn’t include access to an online bookstore, but with a 4.26-inch screen, you can slip it in a pocket alongside your phone. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter

Months after reviewing it, I’m still a huge fan of Valve’s second-generation Steam Controller. It’s comfortable to hold for hours-long gaming sessions, has enough battery life that I never really think about it, and I love how I can customize nearly everything about the controller on a per-game basis inside Steam. If I have one knock against the controller, it’s that I don’t use the big touchpads all that often to replicate a mouse — but I have used them as giant buttons, which can be surprisingly useful in a pinch. I think I’ll be gaming with it for years to come.— Jay Peters, senior reporter

The Peak Design City Bags offer a unique way to hang them up wherever you are. They have a hook so you can hang them off a table and keep them off the dirty ground. The Verge’s Thomas Ricker, who reviewed the bags, said they made him a convert: “It beats setting a bag on the dirty ground or hanging it off the back of the chair where it will inevitably slide onto the floor, and it’s far better than holding a bag on your sweaty lap on a hot summer day.” He said they fit squarely in the everyday carry sweet spot for most people. — Jay Peters, senior reporter

I love ridiculous laptops, and there’s nothing quite as over-the-top as dual-screen models like Asus’ Zephyrus Duo and Zenbook Duo. The wildly expensive Zephyrus Duo gaming laptop is the perfect embodiment of this extravagant formula, with a mobile RTX 5090 GPU, dual 16-inch OLEDs, and a $5,500 price tag. It’s a marvel of maximalism. The more practical version is the latest Zenbook Duo — with its pair of 14-inch OLEDs and Intel Panther Lake chip — which is still pricey at $2,700, but no slouch for 1080p gaming on its integrated GPU. I wish these kinds of laptops had more accessible price points because they are an absolute treat to use. The more screens, the merrier. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer

The Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 power bank is the latest update in its line of ultralight battery packs. Nitecore has made a name for itself among endurance athletes and backpackers who want to pack as light as possible while still having enough power to recharge a phone and a smartwatch. The NB10000 has IPX7 protection to withstand rain or light immersion, two USB-C ports, a 10,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, and enough juice to top up an iPhone 15 Pro twice. It costs $84, which is a lot more than what you’d spend on a standard 10,000mAh battery, but it’s worth it for anyone who wants a thin and light battery that lasts. Oh, and did we mention there are RGB lights around the USB-C ports? — Todd Haselton, deputy reviews editor

Few products are truly perfect all-rounders in the smart home world, but Aqara’s G400 video doorbell comes close. It works with every platform, has local storage, and offers on-device AI to alert you to people at your door. It can record 24/7 because it’s hardwired, which also makes it a good choice for reliability, and there’s even the option of power over ethernet. It looks like a giant Mars bar on my front door, but I can forgive it for this because it does everything else very well. And at only $100, it is one of those rarities in tech today: a good product that’s affordable. — Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer

The Schlage Sense Pro is the smartest lock on the block, thanks to ultra-wideband hands-free unlocking. With your phone in your pocket or bag, it can unlock as you approach, so you can just open the door — no need for keys or fiddling with an app. It’s like stepping into the future. While there are a couple of other UWB locks out there, the Schlage is my favorite because of its sleek, all-metal design, lack of a keyhole, and a very discreet keypad. Today, it works only with Apple Home Key for that magical unlocking, but thanks to its support for Aliro, the new smart lock standard, it should work with Android phones very soon. Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer
